title: Recursion basics
overview: Module 18 introduces recursion: a function that calls itself on a smaller version of the same job. Every recursive function needs a base case that stops the calls, and a recursive step that moves towards that base case. Where you put the work (before or after the recursive call) decides the order of the output.

concepts.explain: The condition where the function returns without calling itself again. If it is missing, the calls never end and the program crashes with a stack overflow.
The call to itself with a smaller or closer problem, such as `x + 1`, `n - 1` or `i + 1`.
Printing before the recursive call prints in the order the calls are made: 1, 2, 3, …
Printing after the call happens while the calls are returning, so the order is reversed: …, 3, 2, 1.
Each call gets its own copy of its parameters, stored on the stack. A call waits until the call it made has returned.
A recursive function can build its answer from the smaller answer: `sum(i) = a[i] + sum(i + 1)`.

files.title: Print 1..N recursively
files.what: `print_1_to_N(x, n)` prints `x` and then asks itself to print from `x + 1` onwards.
steps: `main` reads `n` and starts the chain at `x = 1`.
files.output_note: `Enter the value of n: 1 2 3 4 5`. The prompt and the numbers are on the same line because the typed input isn't shown.

check.q: How many calls happen in total for n = 5?
check.a: 6. That is x = 1 to 5, plus the call with x = 6 that hits the base case.

files.title: Print N..1 recursively
files.what: The same function with the print moved after the call, which reverses the order.
steps: The deepest call (x = n) prints first, and x = 1 prints last.

check.q: Which line decides whether the output goes up or down?
check.a: Where the `printf` sits: before the recursive call or after it.

files.title: Sum of an array recursively
files.what: `getSum(i, n)` returns `a[i]` plus the sum of the rest of the array. Past the end, the sum is 0.
steps: `a` is a global array, filled from input.
Base case: `i == n` returns 0, because nothing is left to add.
files.watch_out: The total is an `int`. With large values, use `long long`.

check.q: What does `getSum(3, 5)` return for this input?

files.title: Print Recursion
files.what: Prints the message `n` times by printing it once and then recursing with `n - 1`.
files.output_note: Three lines of `I love Recursion`, which matches the expected answer.

check.a: The base case `n == 0` is never reached, so the calls go on until the stack overflows. `n <= 0` would be a safer test.

files.title: Print 1 to N (one per line)
files.what: Uses the same pattern as `recursion_print_1_to_N.c`, but prints each number on its own line and shows no prompt, as a judge requires.
files.output_note: `1`, `2`, `3` and `4`, each on its own line.

check.q: What is the difference from the lesson file, and why does it matter?
check.a: It has no prompt and uses newlines. A judge compares output exactly, so an extra prompt would be judged wrong.

files.title: Print N to 1 (no trailing space)
files.what: Recurses first and prints on the way back. It leaves the space off after the last number, which is `1`.
steps: Then print `x`: with a trailing space if `x > 1`, and without one for `x == 1`, which is printed last.
files.output_note: `5 4 3 2 1`, with no space at the end.

check.q: Why is `x == 1` the right case to leave out the space?
check.a: Output goes from high to low, so 1 is always the last number printed.

files.title: Add (with a function)
files.what: `int sum(int x, int y)` returns `x + y`, and `main` prints the result.
steps: Read `x` and `y`. The program prints a prompt first.
files.output_note: `Enter two numbers: 7`. The answer 7 is correct, but it comes after the prompt.
files.watch_out: **The judge would reject this:** the `printf("Enter two numbers: ")` prompt is extra output. Remove it before submitting.

check.a: No. It is a plain function that returns a value.

files.title: Swap (with a function)
files.what: `swap(int *x, int *y)` exchanges the values through pointers, and `main` passes `&x` and `&y`.

check.q: What would print if `swap` took `int x, int y` instead of pointers?
check.a: `5 2`, unchanged, because the function would only swap its copies.

recap: Every recursive function needs a base case and a step that moves towards it.
Printing before the call gives increasing order. Printing after it gives decreasing order.
Each call has its own parameters on the call stack.
A recursive function can build its return value from a smaller call: `a[i] + sum(i+1)`.
On judges, print only what the problem asks for: no prompts.

check_yourself.q: What happens when a recursive function has no reachable base case?
check_yourself.a: It keeps calling itself until the stack runs out and the program crashes.

check_yourself.q: For `f(x){ if(x > 3) return; f(x+1); printf("%d", x); }` called as `f(1)`, what is printed?
Write the base case for a recursive factorial.

body: Take a job you could already do with a loop: print a line five times. Now describe it in a different way, in plain words.

Printing the line five times is the same as printing it once, and then printing it four times. And printing it four times is printing it once, then printing it three times. Keep going and the job shrinks by one each time until there is nothing left to do:
intro.trace:
print 5 times = print once, then print 4 times
print 4 times = print once, then print 3 times
print 3 times = print once, then print 2 times
print 2 times = print once, then print 1 time
print 1 time  = print once, then print 0 times
print 0 times = nothing to do   <-- it stops here

body: Every line but the last describes the job in terms of a **smaller copy of the same job**. The last line is different: it is the size at which you stop. That last line is called the **base case**, and it is the part beginners leave out.
A function is allowed to call itself, so those two lines turn straight into code. This is **recursion**:
What is new here is only that: until now a function called some **other** function, and the work sat in a loop. Now a function hands part of its own job back to itself.

The computer does not merge the calls. Each call is a fresh, separate run of the function with its own `n`, and it is paused while the call it made is running. Trace `show(3)`, indenting one step for each new call:
intro.trace:
show(3)  prints, then calls
  show(2)  prints, then calls
    show(1)  prints, then calls
      show(0)  n is 0, returns at once
    show(1) is finished, returns
  show(2) is finished, returns
show(3) is finished, returns

body: The calls stack up on the way in and unwind on the way out. Now remove `if(n == 0) return;` and follow the same picture: `n` goes 0, then -1, then -2, and the stack keeps growing until the program dies. A recursive function without a base case, or with a step that does not move towards it, never stops.

**A second example, with a value coming back.** The sum of an array from position `i` onwards is `a[i]` plus the sum from position `i+1` onwards, and the sum starting past the last element is 0. So the answers are built on the way back up the stack, not on the way down:
intro.trace:
a = 5 2 7,  getSum(0, 3)
  5 + getSum(1, 3)
      2 + getSum(2, 3)
          7 + getSum(3, 3)
              returns 0
          returns 7
      returns 9
  returns 14

body: **A third example, and the one that catches people.** Where you put the work decides the order of the output. Printing `x` before the call prints on the way down, so the numbers come out 1, 2, 3, 4. Moving the same `printf` after the call prints on the way back up, so the same function now prints 4, 3, 2, 1 without a single change to the counting:

Recursion does not make a program faster; a loop would do all of this. It is worth learning because some jobs really are built out of smaller copies of themselves, and writing those as loops is painful. Later, when you meet trees and graphs, this is the natural way to walk them.
The programs below do exactly these shapes: print 1 to N, print N to 1, and sum an array, each traced call by call, followed by the five practice problems.
